transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-20
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park, Marco Ruiz (Redwood); Priya Singh, Tom Reynolds, Elena Martinez (Novafinance)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Lena, AE on the Redwood side, and Marco our solutions engineer is here to run through Optimize — batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations and a rough cost model. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Priya Singh: Good, thanks. Excited — we've been looking at token costs creeping up for our chat assistant, so hopefully some good wins here.
[00:18] Tom Reynolds: Yep, we want to understand latency tradeoffs too, we can't blow SLA for customer-facing flows.
[00:24] Marco Ruiz: Totally. Quick agenda: we'll cover how Redwood's batching works, prefix vs KV cache patterns, show a simple cost model using your expected qps and avg tokens, and then outline next steps for a pilot.
[00:36] Elena Martinez: Also want to flag security questions up front — encryption, KMS, audit logs and VPC are important for us.
[00:43] Lena Park: Great callout. We'll cover those briefly and attach SOC2 / KMS docs after.

[02:02] Marco Ruiz: Ok starting with batching — the simple intuition: batching groups concurrent inference requests into a single GPU pass to amortize compute. For chatlike workloads with short prompts, you can see 2-6x cost reductions depending on how bursty traffic is. Two levers: batch window (how long we wait to collect requests) and max batch size.
[02:30] Tom Reynolds: Can you quantify 2-6x? Our SLA is 200ms p50 and 500ms p95 for quick customer messages.
[02:38] Marco Ruiz: Right — if you set a 15ms micro-batching window and your concurrency is 20, you might push latency p95 to ~250-300ms but reduce per-token GPU time by ~50%. If you need strict 200ms p95, you reduce window and lose some batching gains. It's always a latency vs cost knob.
[03:05] Priya Singh: Our traffic is bursty — end of month, heavy spikes. Does Redwood support dynamic batching policies?
[03:12] Marco Ruiz: Yes we have autoscaling and dynamic batching. We tune batch size and window based on observed concurrency and latency SLOs. Also there's continuous batching that adapts to sequence length distribution to avoid padding waste.

[04:05] Marco Ruiz: Next, prefix vs KV cache. Prefix cache stores the model's outputs for identical prefixes (like the system instructions + conversation history up to a point) so you can avoid re-computing for repeated starts. KV cache is a token-level cache for key-value pairs in the transformer — that helps when users have similar long histories where the KV state repeats.
[04:27] Lena Park: In practice, prefix cache is great for templated prompts and system messages, KV cache is more powerful for multi-turn sessions where the first N tokens repeat.
[04:35] Tom Reynolds: So for our use case — customers with recurring session templates but different user inputs — prefix cache makes sense?
[04:42] Marco Ruiz: Exactly. If most of the tokens are the same across requests, prefix cache hit rate could be 40-70% in some setups, which directly reduces GPU work. If you have many unique user utterances but similar system prompts, prefix caching still helps on the fixed portion.

[06:10] Marco Ruiz: Important caveat: cache hit rate assumptions drive the cost model. We typically model conservative, base, and optimistic hit rates: 10-20% (conservative), 35-50% (base), 60%+ (optimistic). We'll plug Novafinance numbers in the spreadsheet.
[06:30] Priya Singh: How do you measure hit rate before deploying? We can sample logs but not sure how representative staging traffic is.
[06:37] Marco Ruiz: We recommend a lightweight traffic replay from prod (anonymized) to run through Redwood's estimator or run a short 48-hour shadow test to get real hit rates. That'll be a next step if you want.

[08:00] Marco Ruiz: Cost model overview: tokens per request * avg seq length * request volume gives raw tokens. Then GPU seconds per token (depends on model and quantization) times tokens minus cache savings gives compute. Then add networking, memory, and per-instance overhead. We'll show a worked example.
[08:25] Lena Park: Quick note — we support quantization profiles; moving from fp16 to 4-bit can reduce GPU memory and sometimes cost by ~30% for some models, but you should validate quality on your prompts.
[08:40] Priya Singh: We are sensitive to hallucinations so we want to validate quality first.

[10:00] Marco Ruiz: Alright here's a simplified worked example for Novafinance: assume 50k requests/day, avg input 120 tokens, avg output 80 tokens -> 200 tokens per request. At base model cost on an H100/4-bit path, GPU seconds per 1k tokens ~ X (transcription note: exact kernel numbers approximated in call). If you get a 40% prefix cache hit, effective tokens dropped to 120 tokens per request on average, reducing compute proportionally.
[10:31] Tom Reynolds: Can you show numbers for p50/p95 latency with caching enabled?
[10:36] Marco Ruiz: Sure — rough numbers: no batching, no cache: p50 80ms, p95 260ms on a dedicated small pool; with batching (15ms window) p50 95ms, p95 300ms if concurrency low; with prefix cache hits we often see p50 improve because shorter decoding, p95 depends on tail concurrency. These are approximations; we'll run targeted bench for your traffic.

[12:10] Elena Martinez: On the security front: if we do prefix caching, how do you handle PII? We can't cache sensitive customer data.
[12:18] Marco Ruiz: Good question. We support configurable cache policies: include/exclude rules and token scrubbing. For Private deployments you can opt to keep caches on customer-managed volumes with KMS keys. For Hosted we store caches encrypted at rest and you can enable purge policies. We'll include details in the security pack.
[12:36] Priya Singh: Are there audit logs for cache hits and evictions?
[12:40] Lena Park: Yes per-request traces, cache hit metrics, and eviction logs are available in Redwood Console; can be sent to your SIEM via webhooks.

[14:05] Marco Ruiz: Back to cost model — example spreadsheet (we shared a link) has rows for tokens, effective tokens after cache, GPU seconds, hourly instance cost, amortized per-request cost, and end-to-end per-token cost. Small changes in cache hit rate can swing cost by 20-50% in many cases.
[14:28] Tom Reynolds: You mentioned routing policies earlier. If our traffic is in EU and US, can Redwood route by latency/cost?
[14:35] Marco Ruiz: Yes — we support policy-based routing: latency-first (closest region), cost-first (cheapest compatible model/region), or custom. We can also define fallbacks to smaller model variants or cached replies under load.

[16:05] Priya Singh: For a pilot, we likely want a hosted POC with a dedicated pool for predictable latency. Is that recommended?
[16:12] Marco Ruiz: That's common — a small dedicated pool to hit your p95 targets plus a hosted fallback for burst capacity. That keeps cost predictable while avoiding dropped requests.

[18:00] Marco Ruiz: Now some nuance on KV cache — it's more complex to support but gives benefits when sessions are multi-turn and many tokens are repeated. Complexity: memory needs on the GPU and eviction policy. We can quantify memory footprint — again we'll run bench with your prompt set.
[18:22] Tom Reynolds: Memory bump concerns us — we have some older instance types in our infra. Which GPUs do you recommend?
[18:28] Marco Ruiz: H100 for highest throughput and best 4-bit kernels; A100 still works well and is cheaper in some regions. We'll show per-region instance pricing in the model.

[20:00] Marco Ruiz: A demo of the spreadsheet: (link shared) shows base case: 50k/day, 200 tokens -> base cost $X/day. With 40% prefix cache -> $Y/day. With batching policies tuned -> additional savings. We also show sensitivity to p95 constraints because reducing batching window reduces savings.
[21:10] Priya Singh: Can the Console simulate these?
[21:15] Lena Park: We have an Optimizer view that suggests batch/window settings and estimated savings; it's based on prior deployments but we'll validate. The Console will also surface per-route token/cost breakdown so you can see which flows are expensive.

[23:00] Marco Ruiz: Quick call-outs: cold-start for KV cache, cache warmup time, and TTLs. For interactive chat, a short TTL with high hit-rate prefixes works best. Also, we recommend a hybrid approach — prefix cache for the system + template tokens and KV cache for long-lived sessions where user history repeats.

[24:40] Tom Reynolds: Any red flags — like worst-case cost surprises?
[24:45] Marco Ruiz: Worst-case is low cache hit rate plus large batching windows causing latency misses; we mitigate with SLO-aware routing and can set hard latency caps that bypass batching for specific routes. Also we monitor quality regressions if you change quantization; we recommend an eval suite pre/post changes.

[26:00] Priya Singh: On compliance, we need SOC2 and data residency in EU. Do you have EU regions and can we keep data in region?
[26:08] Lena Park: Yes, we have EU regions and private VPC options. Data residency for logs and caches can be kept in-region with Private deployment. We'll include the region map in follow-up.

[28:10] Marco Ruiz: Ok, sample pilot plan: 1) baseline measurement (48-hour traffic replay), 2) small dedicated pool + optimize config, 3) 2-week pilot with monitoring and cost/quality evaluation, 4) decide on longer reserved capacity. Estimated timeline 3-6 weeks.
[28:36] Tom Reynolds: That fits our timeline — we want to do a pilot before end of Q2.

[30:00] Priya Singh: For the baseline, do you need full prompts or can we anonymize?
[30:06] Marco Ruiz: Anonymized is fine; we mainly need token lengths and token distributions plus a representative prompt set for quality evals.

[31:20] Elena Martinez: A few security Qs: SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS for key ownership, and retention policies.
[31:28] Lena Park: We support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, optional customer-managed KMS for Private, and configurable retention/archival. We'll attach the security pack.

[33:00] Marco Ruiz: Walkthrough of a couple of scenarios in the console (screen sharing hearing note): showing per-route token breakdown, suggested batch windows, cache hit visualizations. (transcription: screen share, pointer to chart).
[34:10] Priya Singh: The chart shows a big % of tokens in the system prompt — that aligns with our suspicion. If we can cache that portion we'd save a lot.
[34:18] Marco Ruiz: Yep exactly — caching system prompt and boilerplate reduces repeated forward compute.

[36:00] Marco Ruiz: Another thing — we sometimes suggest micro-batching for low-latency paths and larger batching for background/async flows. You can tag routes in the console.
[36:12] Tom Reynolds: Good idea. We have async reporting flows that can tolerate higher p95.

[37:50] Marco Ruiz: Now quick note about model variants — for fallback we can serve a smaller/cheaper model in high-load and degrade gracefully. For finance domain you may want to keep a higher quality model for risk-sensitive flows.
[38:05] Priya Singh: We'll want guardrails around which flows can fallback.
[38:08] Lena Park: We can set route-level policies and policies tied to user segments.

[39:30] Marco Ruiz: Wrapping up the cost model: final recommended pilot configuration in spreadsheet: dedicated 2-GPU pool on A100, batching window 10-15ms for interactive, prefix cache TTL 30 minutes for templated tokens, KV cache enabled for sessions flagged as long-lived. Estimated cost reduction 35-45% vs naive no-cache/no-batch baseline depending on hit rates.
[40:02] Tom Reynolds: That reduction is attractive. Any up-front engineering work on our side?
[40:08] Marco Ruiz: Minimal: instrument traffic capture, tag routes for different SLOs, and integrate with our SDK for route-level metadata. For prefix cache you may need to standardize the system prompt and where dynamic user tokens live.

[41:30] Priya Singh: About SDKs — do you have examples for our Node backend?
[41:35] Lena Park: Yes we have Node + Python + Java examples and prompt engineering templates. We'll share repo links.

[42:50] Elena Martinez: Last security Q — can we run pilot in our VPC or do we need Private deployment?
[42:57] Lena Park: For pilot we can host in Redwood's hosted but with dedicated pools and encrypted caches; if you want VPC-level isolation we'd move to Private which takes longer. We'll propose both options in the pilot scope.

[44:20] Marco Ruiz: Ok next steps recap — Lena will send pricing and the pilot scope doc; Marco will run the initial cost model and schedule a 48-hour replay test; Priya will share anonymized prompt set and traffic metrics.
[44:40] Priya Singh: Sounds good. We'll try to get the data to you by Tuesday.

[46:00] Tom Reynolds: Can you also include a rough estimate for reserved capacity discounts?
[46:07] Lena Park: Yes we'll include committed pricing tiers in the pilot proposal.

[47:30] Marco Ruiz: Quick QA: any other blockers?
[47:33] Priya Singh: Not on our side. Need to confirm legal on data processing agreement, but security looks ok so far.
[47:40] Elena Martinez: Legal will want the DPIA and DPA drafts.
[47:45] Lena Park: We'll loop in our legal and send the templates.

[49:00] Marco Ruiz: Final note — we'll also provide an evaluation harness so you can run automatic quality checks when changing quantization or model variants.
[49:12] Priya Singh: Appreciate that.

[50:00] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the documents and calendar invite for the pilot planning.
[50:08] Tom Reynolds: Thanks.
[50:10] Priya Singh: Thanks all.
[51:00] (call ends)
